claim: SARS-CoV-2 is the agent of a major global outbreak of respiratory tract disease known as Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19).
source: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the agent of a major global outbreak of respiratory tract disease known as Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infects mainly lungs.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infects mainly lungs and may cause several immune-related complications, such as lymphocytopenia and cytokine storm, which are associated with the severity of the disease and predict mortality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 infection.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may cause lymphocytopenia.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infects mainly lungs and may cause several immune-related complications, such as lymphocytopenia and cytokine storm, which are associated with the severity of the disease and predict mortality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 complications.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may cause cytokine storm.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infects mainly lungs and may cause several immune-related complications, such as lymphocytopenia and cytokine storm, which are associated with the severity of the disease and predict mortality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 complications.

claim: Lymphocytopenia and cytokine storm are associated with the severity of COVID-19 disease and predict mortality.
source: SARS-CoV-2 infects mainly lungs and may cause several immune-related complications, such as lymphocytopenia and cytokine storm, which are associated with the severity of the disease and predict mortality.
evidence: This is established knowledge about COVID-19 disease severity markers.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infects human CD4+ T helper cells.
source: Here, we show that SARS-CoV-2 infects human CD4+ T helper cells, but not CD8+ T cells, and is present in blood and bronchoalveolar lavage T helper cells of severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including RT-qPCR, in situ hybridization, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy (Figure 1).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 does not infect CD8+ T cells.
source: Here, we show that SARS-CoV-2 infects human CD4+ T helper cells, but not CD8+ T cells, and is present in blood and bronchoalveolar lavage T helper cells of severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing viral RNA was detected in CD4+ T cells but not CD8+ T cells (Figure 1A).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is present in blood T helper cells of severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Here, we show that SARS-CoV-2 infects human CD4+ T helper cells, but not CD8+ T cells, and is present in blood and bronchoalveolar lavage T helper cells of severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in CD4+ T cells from peripheral blood of COVID-19 patients (Figure 1F).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is present in bronchoalveolar lavage T helper cells of severe COVID-19 patients.
source: Here, we show that SARS-CoV-2 infects human CD4+ T helper cells, but not CD8+ T cells, and is present in blood and bronchoalveolar lavage T helper cells of severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing SARS-CoV-2 RNA in CD4+ T cells from bronchoalveolar lavage (Figure 1G).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein (S) directly binds to the CD4 molecule.
source: We demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein (S) directly binds to the CD4 molecule, which in turn mediates the entry of SARS- CoV-2 in T helper cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 3A) and fluorescence anisotropy binding assays (Figure 3B, C).

claim: CD4 mediates the entry of SARS-CoV-2 in T helper cells.
source: We demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein (S) directly binds to the CD4 molecule, which in turn mediates the entry of SARS- CoV-2 in T helper cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments showing that blocking CD4 with antibodies or soluble CD4 reduces viral load (Figure 3D, E), and that CD4 expression increases viral infection (Figure 3F, H).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection leads to impaired CD4 T cell function.
source: This leads to impaired CD4 T cell function and may cause cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data showing alterations in multiple cellular pathways (Figure 4A, B) and changes in cytokine expression (Figure 4C, D).

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection may cause CD4 T cell death.
source: This leads to impaired CD4 T cell function and may cause cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data showing changes in apoptosis-related proteins (Figure 4A, B) and viability assays showing reduced cell viability (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected T helper cells express higher levels of IL-10.
source: SARS-CoV-2-infected T helper cells express higher levels of IL-10, which is associated with viral persistence and disease severity.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data showing increased IL-10 expression in infected CD4+ T cells (Figure 4D) and in cells from severe COVID-19 patients (Figure 4C).

claim: IL-10 expression is associated with viral persistence.
source: SARS-CoV-2-infected T helper cells express higher levels of IL-10, which is associated with viral persistence and disease severity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on IL-10 and viral persistence (Brooks et al., 2006).

claim: IL-10 expression is associated with COVID-19 disease severity.
source: SARS-CoV-2-infected T helper cells express higher levels of IL-10, which is associated with viral persistence and disease severity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing higher IL-10 expression in severe COVID-19 patients (Figure 4C) and citations to literature (Han et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020).

claim: CD4-mediated SARS-CoV-2 infection of T helper cells may contribute to a poor immune response in COVID-19 patients.
source: Thus, CD4-mediated SARS-CoV-2 infection of T helper cells may contribute to a poor immune response in COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing CD4+ T cell infection, dysfunction, and altered cytokine expression.

claim: COVID-19 has caused millions of deaths around the world.
source: COVID-19 has caused millions of deaths around the world.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the COVID-19 pandemic.

claim: Most COVID-19 deaths are associated with acute pneumonia, cardiovascular complications, and organ failure due to hypoxia, exacerbated inflammatory responses, and widespread cell death.
source: Most of the deaths are associated with acute pneumonia, cardiovascular complications, and organ failure due to hypoxia, exacerbated inflammatory responses, and widespread cell death (Candido et al., 2020; Laing et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020; Moore and June, 2020; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Individuals that progress to severe stages of COVID-19 manifest marked alterations in the immune response, characterized by reduced overall protein synthesis, cytokine storm, lymphocytopenia, and T cell exhaustion.
source: Individuals that progress to the severe stages of COVID-19 manifest marked alterations in the immune response, characterized by reduced overall protein synthesis, cytokine storm, lymphocytopenia, and T cell exhaustion (Arunachalam et al., 2020; De Biasi et al., 2020; Moore and June, 2020; Thoms et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A considerable proportion of infected individuals present low titers of neutralizing antibodies.
source: In addition to these acute effects on the immune system, a considerable proportion of infected individuals present low titers of neutralizing antibodies (Robbiani et al., 2020; Souza et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The levels of antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 decay rapidly after recovery in part of the infected individuals.
source: Moreover, the levels of antibodies against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) decay rapidly after recovery in part of the infected individuals (Long et al., 2020), suggesting that SARS-CoV-2 infection may exert profound and long-lasting complications to adaptive immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection may exert profound and long-lasting complications to adaptive immunity.
source: Moreover, the levels of antibodies against severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) decay rapidly after recovery in part of the infected individuals (Long et al., 2020), suggesting that SARS-CoV-2 infection may exert profound and long-lasting complications to adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of rapid antibody decay.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is able to infect lymphocytes.
source: Recently, it has been shown that SARS-CoV-2 is able to infect lymphocytes (Pontelli et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the canonical mechanism of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the spike glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 binds to the host angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), after which it is cleaved by TMPRSS2.
source: In what has been proposed to be the canonical mechanism of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the spike glycoprotein of SARS-CoV-2 (sCoV-2) binds to the host angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), after which it is cleaved by TMPRSS2 (Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TMPRSS2 is ubiquitously expressed in human tissues.
source: While TMPRSS2 is ubiquitously expressed in human tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), ACE2 is mainly expressed in epithelial and endothelial cells, as well as in the kidney, testis, and small intestine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ACE2 is mainly expressed in epithelial and endothelial cells, as well as in the kidney, testis, and small intestine.
source: While TMPRSS2 is ubiquitously expressed in human tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), ACE2 is mainly expressed in epithelial and endothelial cells, as well as in the kidney, testis, and small intestine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A wide variety of cell types are potentially infected by SARS-CoV-2.
source: Still, a wide variety of cell types are potentially infected by SARS-CoV-2 (Codo et al., 2020; Crunfli et al., 2022; Lamers et al., 2020; de Oliveira et al., 2022; Pascoal et al., 2021; Saccon et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2020), even though some of these cells express very low levels of ACE2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some cell types infected by SARS-CoV-2 express very low levels of ACE2.
source: Still, a wide variety of cell types are potentially infected by SARS-CoV-2 (Codo et al., 2020; Crunfli et al., 2022; Lamers et al., 2020; de Oliveira et al., 2022; Pascoal et al., 2021; Saccon et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2020), even though some of these cells express very low levels of ACE2.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lymphocytes express very low levels of ACE2.
source: We showed that this is the case for lymphocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Binding of sCoV-2 to certain cell surface proteins facilitates viral entry.
source: In agreement with the latter, binding of sCoV-2 to certain cell surface proteins facilitates viral entry (Cantuti-Castelvetri et al., 2020; Cecon et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The structures of the spike of SARS-CoV-1 (sCoV-1) and the sCoV-2 proteins are similar.
source: Since the structures of the spike of SARS-CoV-1 (sCoV-1) and the sCoV-2 proteins are similar (Wrapp et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020), we used the P-HIPSTer algorithm to uncover human proteins that putatively interact with spike (Lasso et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Seventy-one human proteins were predicted to interact with sCoV-1 by the P-HIPSTer algorithm.
source: Seventy-one human proteins were predicted to interact with sCoV-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational prediction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: CD4 was the only protein predicted to interact with sCoV-1 that appeared in all five databases of plasma membrane proteins.
source: CD4 was the only protein predicted to interact with sCoV-1 that appeared in all five databases (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by database cross-referencing analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: CD4 is expressed mainly in T helper lymphocytes.
source: CD4 is expressed mainly in T helper lymphocytes and has been shown to be the co-receptor to HIV (Shaik et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD4 expression.

claim: CD4 has been shown to be the co-receptor to HIV.
source: CD4 is expressed mainly in T helper lymphocytes and has been shown to be the co-receptor to HIV (Shaik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CD4+ T lymphocytes orchestrate innate and adaptive immune response.
source: Since CD4+ T lymphocytes orchestrate innate and adaptive immune response (Gasteiger and Rudensky, 2014; O'Shea and Paul, 2010), infection of CD4+ T cells by SARS-CoV-2 could explain lymphocytopenia and dysregulated inflammatory response in severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Infection of CD4+ T cells represents an effective mechanism for viruses to escape the immune response.
source: Moreover, from an evolutionary perspective, infection of CD4+ T cells represents an effective mechanism for viruses to escape the immune response (Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in CD4+ T cells 24 hours post infection.
source: We were able to detect SARS-CoV-2 RNA in CD4+ T cells, but not CD8+ T cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA was not detected in CD8+ T cells 24 hours post infection.
source: We were able to detect SARS-CoV-2 RNA in CD4+ T cells, but not CD8+ T cells (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The amount of SARS-CoV-2 RNA remains roughly stable until 48 hr post infection in CD4+ T cells.
source: Notably, the amount of SARS-CoV-2 RNA remains roughly stable until 48 hr post infection (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-course RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CD4+ T cells were infected by the P.1 (gamma) variant of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Of note, although most of the data presented here was generated using the ancient SARS-CoV-2 B lineage, CD4+ T cells were also infected by the P.1 (gamma) variant (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: The negative strand (antisense) of SARS-CoV-2 was detected in infected CD4+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, we identified the presence of the negative strand (antisense) of SARS-CoV-2 in the infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), demonstrating that the virus replicates in T helper cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 replicates in T helper cells.
source: Furthermore, we identified the presence of the negative strand (antisense) of SARS-CoV-2 in the infected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D), demonstrating that the virus replicates in T helper cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the detection of the negative strand, which is an indicator of viral replication.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected CD4+ T cells release infectious viral particles.
source: We also found by plaque assay analysis that SARS-CoV-2-infected CD4+ T cells release infectious viral particles, although much less efficiently than Vero cells (positive control) (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SARS-CoV-2-infected CD4+ T cells release infectious viral particles much less efficiently than Vero cells.
source: We also found by plaque assay analysis that SARS-CoV-2-infected CD4+ T cells release infectious viral particles, although much less efficiently than Vero cells (positive control) (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by plaque assay data comparing CD4+ T cells and Vero cells shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 RNA was detected in 2.1% of CD4+ T cells of the bronchoalveolar lavage of patients with severe COVID-19.
source: Using publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) data (Liao et al., 2020), we detected the presence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in 2.1% of CD4+ T cells of the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) of patients with severe COVID-19 (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Molecular docking analyses predicted that sCoV-2 receptor binding domain (RBD) directly interacts with the N-terminal domain (NTD) of CD4 Ig-like V type.
source: Based on the putative interaction found using P-HIPSTer, we performed molecular docking analyses and predicted that sCoV-2 receptor binding domain (RBD) directly interacts with the N-terminal domain (NTD) of CD4 Ig-like V type (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational molecular docking data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two models remained stable after molecular dynamics simulations at 353 K and represent likely candidates for the interaction between the CD4 NTD and sCoV-2 RBD.
source: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with stepwise temperature increase were applied to challenge the kinetic stability of the docking model representatives (Figure 2B). Two models remained stable after the third step of simulation at 353 K and represent likely candidates for the interaction between the CD4 NTD and sCoV-2 RBD (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The interaction region of RBD with CD4 is predicted to overlap with that of human ACE2.
source: The interaction region of RBD with CD4 is predicted to overlap with that of human ACE2 (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The interaction between CD4 and sCoV-2 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation.
source: The interaction between CD4 and sCoV-2 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RBD and CD4 interact with high affinity (Kd = 22 nM).
source: Binding affinity isotherms, obtained by fluorescence anisotropy assay, confirmed the physical high-affinity interaction between RBD and CD4 (Kd = 22 nM) and spike full length and CD4 (Kd = 27 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Spike full length and CD4 interact with high affinity (Kd = 27 nM).
source: Binding affinity isotherms, obtained by fluorescence anisotropy assay, confirmed the physical high-affinity interaction between RBD and CD4 (Kd = 22 nM) and spike full length and CD4 (Kd = 27 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The interaction interface between sCoV-2 and CD4 occurs at the RBD.
source: Considering the similar affinities, these results suggest that the interaction interface between sCoV-2 and CD4 occurs at the RBD (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similar binding affinities of RBD and full-length spike to CD4.

claim: Pre-incubation with soluble CD4 (sCD4) completely blunted viral load in CD4+ T cells exposed to SARS-CoV-2.
source: Consistent with the hypothesis that CD4-sCoV-2 interaction is required for infection, we observed that pre-incubation with soluble CD4 (sCD4) completely blunted viral load in CD4+ T cells exposed to SARS-CoV-2 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing reduced viral load with sCD4 treatment shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CD4 inhibition with monoclonal antibody (RPA-T4) reduced SARS-CoV-2 load in CD4+ T cells.
source: We observed that CD4 inhibition reduced SARS-CoV-2 load (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing reduced viral load with anti-CD4 antibody treatment shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The presence of CD4 was sufficient to increase viral load in A3.01 cells compared to A2.01.
source: Despite expressing higher levels of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 than primary CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the presence of CD4 was sufficient to increase viral load in A3.01 cells compared to A2.01 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data comparing A3.01 and A2.01 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The introduction of CD4 in A2.01 increased viral load.
source: Importantly, the introduction of CD4 in A2.01 increased viral load (Figure 3H and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by viral load data comparing A2.01 and A2.04 (CD4-expressing) cells shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Inhibition of ACE2 using polyclonal antibody diminished SARS-CoV-2 entry in CD4+ T cells.
source: Inhibition of ACE2 using polyclonal antibody (Figure 3I) diminished SARS-CoV-2 entry in CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing reduced viral load with anti-ACE2 antibody treatment shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The inhibition of TMPRSS2 with camostat mesylate reduced SARS-CoV-2 load in CD4+ T cells.
source: Moreover, the inhibition of TMPRSS2 with camostat mesylate reduced SARS-CoV-2 load (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing reduced viral load with camostat mesylate treatment shown in Figure 3J.

claim: ACE2, TMPRSS2, and CD4 are all required to allow the infection of CD4+ T cells by SARS-CoV-2.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that ACE2, TMPRSS2, and CD4 are all required to allow the infection of CD4+ T cells by SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that blocking any of these molecules reduces viral infection.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection alters multiple housekeeping pathways associated with the immune system, infectious diseases, cell cycle, and cellular metabolism in CD4+ T cells.
source: We found that SARS-CoV-2 infection alters multiple housekeeping pathways associated with the immune system, infectious diseases, cell cycle, and cellular metabolism (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry-based shotgun proteomics data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 exposure elicits alterations associated with 'cellular responses to stress' in CD4+ T cells.
source: SARS-CoV-2 exposure elicits alterations associated with 'cellular responses to stress,' which include changes in proteins involved in translation, mitochondrial metabolism, cytoskeleton remodeling, cellular senescence, and apoptosis (Figure 4B and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ex vivo exposure of CD4+ T cells with SARS-CoV-2 resulted in 10% reduction of cell viability 24 hr after infection with a low MOI (0.1).
source: In agreement, ex vivo exposure of CD4+ T cells with SARS-CoV-2 resulted in 10% reduction of cell viability 24 hr after infection with a low MOI (0.1) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3F.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 can induce apoptosis in different cell lines through stimulation of autophagy via inhibition of mTOR signaling.
source: SARS-CoV-2 can induce apoptosis in different cell lines through stimulation of autophagy via inhibition of mTOR signaling (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 can induce inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in primary monocytes and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from COVID-19 patients.
source: It can also induce inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in primary monocytes and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from COVID-19 patients (Alvim et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In epithelial respiratory and kidney cell lines, SARS-CoV drives multimodal necrosis.
source: In epithelial respiratory and kidney cell lines, SARS-CoV drives multimodal necrosis (Yue et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In lymphocytes, apoptosis is the mechanism underlying SARS-CoV-2-mediated cell death.
source: In lymphocytes, however, it has been demonstrated that apoptosis is the mechanism underlying SARS-CoV-2-mediated cell death (Crunfli et al., 2022), which is in line with our proteomic data (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and proteomic data.

claim: IL-10 expression by CD4+ T cells was higher in BAL of severe COVID-19 patients.
source: We found that IL-10 expression by CD4+ T cells was higher in BAL (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and blood (Figure 4C) of severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: IL-10 expression by CD4+ T cells was higher in blood of severe COVID-19 patients.
source: We found that IL-10 expression by CD4+ T cells was higher in BAL (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and blood (Figure 4C) of severe COVID-19 patients.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Purified CD4+ T cells exposed to SARS-CoV-2 expressed higher levels of IL-10.
source: These changes were at least in part cell autonomous since purified CD4+ T cells exposed to SARS-CoV-2 also expressed higher levels of IL-10 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CD4+ T cells from severe COVID-19 patients had decreased expression of IFNγ in relation to cells from patients with the moderate form of the disease or healthy donors.
source: CD4+ T cells from severe COVID-19 patients had decreased expression of IFNγ and IL-17A in relation to cells from patients with the moderate form of the disease or healthy donors (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CD4+ T cells from severe COVID-19 patients had decreased expression of IL-17A in relation to cells from patients with the moderate form of the disease or healthy donors.
source: CD4+ T cells from severe COVID-19 patients had decreased expression of IFNγ and IL-17A in relation to cells from patients with the moderate form of the disease or healthy donors (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The activation of the transcription factor CREB-1 via Ser133 phosphorylation induces IL-10 expression.
source: The activation of the transcription factor CREB-1 via Ser133 phosphorylation induces IL-10 expression (Gee et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CREB-1 phosphorylation at Ser133 was increased in SARS-CoV-2-infected CD4+ T cells.
source: Consistent with IL-10 upregulation, CREB-1 phosphorylation at Ser133 was increased in SARS-CoV-2-infected CD4+ T cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers a signaling cascade that culminates in the upregulation of IL-10 in CD4+ T cells.
source: Thus, SARS-CoV-2 infection triggers a signaling cascade that culminates in the upregulation of IL-10 in CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased CREB-1 phosphorylation and IL-10 expression.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection of CD4+ T cells compromises cell viability.
source: Altogether, our data demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 infects CD4+ T cells, impairs cell function, leads to increased IL-10 expression, and compromises cell viability, which in turn dampens immunity against the virus and contributes to disease severity.
evidence: This claim is supported by viability assay data and proteomic data showing apoptosis-related changes.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection of CD4+ T cells dampens immunity against the virus.
source: Altogether, our data demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 infects CD4+ T cells, impairs cell function, leads to increased IL-10 expression, and compromises cell viability, which in turn dampens immunity against the virus and contributes to disease severity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of infection on CD4+ T cell function and viability.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection of CD4+ T cells contributes to disease severity.
source: Altogether, our data demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 infects CD4+ T cells, impairs cell function, leads to increased IL-10 expression, and compromises cell viability, which in turn dampens immunity against the virus and contributes to disease severity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed effects of infection on CD4+ T cell function and the correlation with disease severity markers.

claim: Impaired innate and adaptive immunity is a hallmark of COVID-19, particularly in patients that progress to the critical stages of the disease.
source: Impaired innate and adaptive immunity is a hallmark of COVID-19, particularly in patients that progress to the critical stages of the disease (Hadjadj et al., 2020; Mathew et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The alterations in immune responses associated with severe COVID-19 are at least partially triggered by infection of CD4+ T helper cells by SARS-CoV-2 and consequent dysregulation of immune function.
source: Here, we propose that the alterations in immune responses associated with severe COVID-19 are at least partially triggered by infection of CD4+ T helper cells by SARS-CoV-2 and consequent dysregulation of immune function.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: T helper cells are infected by SARS-CoV-2 using a mechanism that involves binding of sCoV-2 to CD4 and entry mediated by the canonical ACE2/TMPRSS2 pathway.
source: T helper cells are infected by SARS-CoV-2 using a mechanism that involves binding of sCoV-2 to CD4 and entry mediated by the canonical ACE2/TMPRSS2 pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing CD4 binding, and the requirement of ACE2 and TMPRSS2 for infection.

claim: CD4 stabilizes SARS-CoV-2 on the cell membrane until the virus encounters ACE2 to enter the cell.
source: We propose a model where CD4 stabilizes SARS-CoV-2 on the cell membrane until the virus encounters ACE2 to enter the cell.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the mechanism of infection.

claim: CD4 co-expression with ACE2 in HEK293 cells decreases the affinity and the maximal binding between the sCoV-2 RBD and ACE2.
source: Moreover, Cecon and colleagues showed that CD4 co- expression with ACE2 in HEK293 cells decreases the affinity and the maximal binding between the sCoV-2 RBD and ACE2 (Cecon et al., 2022), which is in line with our MD results and the binding assays (Figure 3), suggesting an intricate mechanism of modulation of SARS- CoV-2 infection in CD4+ T cells (Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In CD4-expressing cells direct binding of sCoV-2 to the CD4 molecule represents a potential mechanism to favor viral entry.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that in CD4-expressing cells direct binding of sCoV-2 to the CD4 molecule represents a potential mechanism to favor viral entry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 in CD4+ T cells leads to protein expression changes consistent with alterations in pathways related to stress response, apoptosis, and cell cycle regulation.
source: Once in CD4+ T cells, SARS-CoV-2 leads to protein expression changes consistent with alterations in pathways related to stress response, apoptosis, and cell cycle regulation, which, if sustained, culminate in cell dysfunction and may lead to cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Sustained alterations in stress response, apoptosis, and cell cycle regulation pathways culminate in cell dysfunction and may lead to cell death.
